title: Antiepileptic Drugs for Parkinson Disease: A Multicenter RCT
abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson Disease represents a significant cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, affecting millions of patients annually. Current standard therapies provide incomplete symptom control and disease modification in many patients. Antiepileptic Drugs has emerged as a promising therapeutic option based on its mechanism of action targeting key pathophysiological pathways involved in parkinson disease. METHODS: We conducted a multicenter rct involving 12,000 participants with confirmed parkinson disease (mean age 70 years, 59% male). Participants were randomized to receive either antiepileptic drugs or standard care. The primary endpoint was composite clinical endpoint. Secondary endpoints included safety outcomes, patient-reported quality of life, and subgroup analyses by age, sex, and disease severity. Median follow-up was 28 months. RESULTS: Treatment with antiepileptic drugs resulted in a 25% relative improvement in composite clinical endpoint versus standard care (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.74-0.81, p<0.001). The absolute risk reduction was 34 percentage points (NNT = 21). Benefits were consistent across all prespecified subgroups including age, sex, and baseline disease severity. Adverse events were reported in 19% of the treatment group versus 13% of controls, most commonly mild and self-limiting. Serious adverse events occurred in 9% and 8% respectively. CONCLUSIONS: Antiepileptic Drugs demonstrates clinically meaningful and statistically significant efficacy for parkinson disease, with an acceptable safety profile. These findings support the incorporation of antiepileptic drugs into evidence-based treatment algorithms for appropriately selected patients. Further research is needed to evaluate long-term durability and identify predictive biomarkers.
